activity_context.topic_title: Differentiating Curves Given in Polar Form

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/dfc16cf0da1332a921899dc1d3ebcdf75a59de3d1323c83f81a61c665b135ea8.png)

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi },$ shown above.
feedback.worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Using the fact that $r=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi },$ we get

$$
x=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{({e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[({e}^{\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={(\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{({e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[({e}^{\theta })^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )] \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }[{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{e}^{\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\frac{{e}^{\theta }}{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$
